Title: Testamenta Eboracensia, or Wills registered at York, illustrative of the history, manners, language, statistics, &c., of the province of York, from the year 1300 downwards (a selection of wills from the registry at York), Vol. III (Publications of the Surtees Society, Vol. 45)
Creator: Will-makers of the Province of York (the wills themselves); selected and edited for the Surtees Society by James Raine and John William Clay (as the host record lists the editors)
Publisher: Durham: the Surtees Society; London: J. B. Nichols and Son (Surtees Society vol. 45)
Publication Date: 1865
Rights: Public Domain
Rights basis: Title page, read in the OCR: 'Surtees Society, Vol. 45' and '1865'; host metadata: date 1865, possible-copyright-status NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.
Language: enm
Source: Internet Archive item testamentaebora05claygoog (archive.org/details/testamentaebora05claygoog), full-text file testamentaebora05claygoog_djvu.txt, fetched directly by the Library thread, October 2026.
Provenance note: Header prepended; the OCR text follows unchanged apart from this header. Google scanning notice left in place. OCR sampled at the opening, the middle and the end: readable Latin and English wills, with many misread letters in the notes. Nothing corrected, re-spaced or retyped.
Content note: Volume III of the Surtees Society's selection of York wills: the wills, in Latin and in English, with the editors' preface and long notes on the testators and their families, and an index. The wills in this volume are wills of about 1380 to 1500, peaking in the 1470s and 1480s. The will-makers' own words, in the form the registry kept. A second witness for exact wording because of the OCR on the early English and Latin; check page images before quoting.

At a General Meeting of the Surtees Societt, held in the 
Castle of Durham, on the 15th of June, 1863, Sir William 
Lawson, Bart., in the chair — it was 

Resolved, That a Third Volume of the Testamenta 
Eboracensia should be prepared by the Secretary, as one of the 
Publications of the Society for 1864. 

JAMES EAINE, 

Secretary.

J. B. mCHOLI AKD SOMt, ^ftlMTSU, Ifo, rAKLlAXlMT tTkXST. 



THE PREFACE. 



A third Tolume of Wills from the Registry at 
York is submitted to the members of the Surtees 
Society. The period of time that it covers, coimting 
from the date at which its predecessor ends, is only^ 
eighteen years^ The number and value of the docu- 
ments preserved at York make a slow progress neces- 
sary. A large space, also, has been devoted to several 
Inventories of a very early date which have been 
recently discovered. The rarity of these lists is only 
equalled by their value. Several will appear in a 
fourth volume, including a magnificent one of Arch- 
bishop Savage. 

It is unnecessary, perhaps, to speak of the value 
and the use of testamentary documents. The light 
which they throw upon language, religious customs 
and observances, and the manners and life of our 
forefathers, is very great indeed. With regard to 
genealogy, it is not too much to say that the three 
volumes of Yorkshire Wills that are already pub- 
lished, buUd up or reconstruct the pedigrees of the 
gentry of that great county. The Editor has ap- 
pended to the present volume a list of the Marriage 
Licences, &c., recorded in the Northern Hegisters. 
He hopes to be able to publish from the same 
sources, on some future occasion, a full catalogue 
of the Indulgences and Licences for Oratories which 
were granted in the North of England. 



VI 



It is the chief object of the Surtees Society, not to 
write history, but to supply the materials out of which 
it can be constructed. The members, however, at all 
times take a great interest in the use, which is being 
constantly made, of the publications of the Society. 
They will be much gratified to hear that considerable 
additions are to be made to the printed works on the 
topography of Yorkshire. The coiinties of Durham and 
Northumberland have found many chroniclers, but the 
vastness of Yorkshire has deterred ahnost every one 
from attempting to elucidate its annals in a similar 
manner. The author of the History of South York- 
shire is an ULustrious exception ; but his is the only 
work that can be spoken of with any respect, as far 
as accuracy and research are concerned. The Editor 
is most happy to announce that there will soon be 
a continuation of the works on Yorkshire topography 
which, in size at least, will range with Mr. Hunter's 
invaluable volumes. The Editor believes, that, if pro- 
perly qualified writers could be found, there would 
be no lack of funds to complete on one plan and in 
one form the history of the whole of Yorkshire, so 
great is the spirit of the gentlemen of that noble 
county. These results are partly owing to the pub- 
lications of the Surtees Society, and the members may 
well be proud of them. The Editor begs them, in the 
name of the Society to which they belong, to assist 
and help on the great work that is in progress. 

J. S;. 

York, June 1865.

* A great and wealthy ecclesiastic. 

On the 14th of March, 1879, Mr. Thomas de Dalby, rector of Barking, exchanged 
his Hying with Laurence de Nayrer for the rectory of Alderton, in the diocese of Nor- 
wich, and the prebend of Welton Beckhall, at Lincoln. (MSS. Harl. 6952, 146.) On 
the 5th of October, 1883, he was presented by John lord Lovel to the rectory of 
Westley, co. Stofford. (F.R.R.) This he exchanged in 1886 for the living of Got- 
tenham, ca Cambridge, which he exchanged again with Thomas de Pattesle for the 
archdeaconry of Ely, to which he was collated May 28th, 1887. He was also rector 
of Stretham, near Ely, and prebendary of Salisbury. (Bentham^s Ely, 275.) In Sept. 
1888, the king appointed him to the archdeaconry of Richmond, at York, and he gave 
up •that of Ely. (Le Ncto, iii. 139.) He was again admitted to Richmond by the 
cluster, during the vacancy of the see, on the 5th of March, 1396-7. (Reg. Deo. et 
Cap. sede vaeante, 2076.) On the 18th of February, 1389, he exchanged his stall 
ot Welton at Lincoln with Robert de Dalton for the prebend of Tockerington at 
York. (MSS. Harl. 6952, 26b,) Dalby was a canon residentiary at York. 

Dalby made his will on the 16th of May, 1400, and it is printed in the lest. Ebor., 
i. 261--4. It was also registered at Canterbury. In the nave of York Minster was '* a 
blue marble, about three yards long, escocheoned at comers, with a coat of arms, a 
chevron between three buckles, and at the head a square plate, with the inscription.** 
(MS. Torre on York Minster, 153.) Dalbv died on the 19th of May, 1400. (Le Neve, 
iii. 189.) In accordance with his last will, a chantry was founded at the altar of 
8S. Agatha, Lucy, and Scholastica, in York Minster, on Jan. 20th, 1409-10, for 
the souls of archdeacon Dalby, archbishop Arundel, Richard Asty, and l»ahel his 
wife, and Sir Philip de Beauchamp. It was worth twelve marks per annum. (York 
Fabric Rolls, 276.)

* Dilapidations claimed by his successor in the archdeaconry, and the residentiaries. 

t Canon of Yorlc 1404—9. See Test. Ebor. i. 853. 

t A very distingaished penon, of whose histoiy bnt little hsa been hitherto 
known. He takes his name from Scarle, a village in Lincolnshire. 

In 1382 he was a clerk of the chanceiy of the higher grade. (Foss^ Judges, iv. 
177.) In 1384 he was a clerk of parliament, and acted as such for many years, and 
in 1382 and for a long while afterwards, yiz. in 1382-7, 1890.8, 1397 and 1399, he 
was a trier of petitions in parliament. (Rot. Pari., iii. var. loc.) On the 22nd of 
July, 1394, he was made master of the rolls, and held that office until Sept. 1396. 
(Newcourt, i. 340. Cal. Rot. Pat, 229. Dugd. Chron. 65.) As such, on August 
10th, 1397, he lent the king 200/. (Fosdera, viii. 9), and on several occasions he had 
the temporary charge of the great seal. (Foss, iv. 177.) From Sept. 1399, to March 
1401, Scarle was lord chancellor of England. (Ibid.) He continued to be a mem- 
ber of the king^s council ; and in Jan. 1403, he and the bishop of Rochester were 
appointed to eicamine into the evidences of Uie alien priories in England, it being 
recommended by the Commons that they should be resumed into the king^ hand. 
(AcU and Ord. of the Privy Council, i. 190.) 

From 1382 to 1385 Scarle was vicar of Desborough, Northanto. (Bridges' North- 
ants, ii. 27.) On the 30th of October, 1385, he was instituted to the rectory of 
Althorp, CO. Lincoln, which he held till 1390. (MSS. Cotton. Nero D. in. 239.) 
On the 13th of February, 1387-8, the king gave him the stall of Ulleskelf at York. 
(Le Neve, iii. 219.) On the 11th of October, 1896, the abbat and convent of West- 
minster presented him to the rectory of St Bride, London. (Newcourt, i. 316.) 
On the 27th of August, 1397, the chapter of York sent him to parliament as their 
proctor (Acta Cap. Ebor.), and on the 19th of September, 1400, he was collated to 
the stall of Weigfaton in that church. He seems also to have been vicar of Northall 
when he died (Newcourt, i. 702), and perhaps he was sometime rector of St. Thomas 
at Winchelsea. (Cooper's Winchelsea, 141.) Between 1401 and 1408 he was arch- 
deacon of Lincoln (Le Neve, ii. 45). and he was also rector for a while of Holme-by- 
the-Sea. (Blomefield's Norfolk, x. 833.) Scarle is said to have been buried in the 
chuTch of St Bride at London. (Willis, i. 177.)

* A flon of Sir John Heron of Eppleden, co. Durham, knight. His first wife was

zabeth, daughter of Thomas Boteler, lord Sudeley. 

Sir William died childless on the 80th of October, 1 iOi. He saw much service 
abroad, and held many state employments. Heniy IV., when he came to the throne,

Z Stephen le Scrope, the son of the testator, arose to some eminence in the Church 
through the influence of his uncle the archbishop. 

On March the 2l8t, 1395-6» whilst his uncle was bishop of Lichfield, he was collated 
to the prebend of Offley in that church, which he gave up in 1397 for that of Colwich. 
This he exchanged on 15th of June, 1400, for the stall of Dernford, which he resigned 
almost immediately. (Le Neve, i. 591, 596, 615.) 

On the 14th of May, 1400, he was appointed chancellor of the university of Cam- 
bridge, and he held the same office in 1414. (Le Neve, iii. 599.) On the^7th of Sep- 
tember in the latter y^r Henry lY. requested him to put an end to the quarrels be- 
tween the masters, regents, and non -regents, and the graduates and scholars in civil 
and canon law. (Feed. xii. 158.) 

In the year 1400 he was beneficed in the diocese of York, and a burst of preferment 
broke all at once upon him. On the 28th of December, 1399, he was collated to the 
stall of Langtoft at York (Reg. Scrope, 2 a), which he held for a twelvemonth. In 
February, 1399-1400, he was made prebendary of Knaresbro\ which he ceded in March 
1401-2. (Ibid.) On the 19th of May, 1400, the archbishop made him archdeacon of 
Richmond on the death of Thomas de Dalby (Ibid. 8 a) ; this honourable post, however, 
went for a short time to Nicholas de Bubwith by papal provision. On the 12th of 
Jnne Scrope was ordained subdeacon, and deacon on the 18th of September. (Reg. 
Scrope.) On the 4th of March, 1400-1, the archbishop collated him to the stall of Drif- 
field, which he exchanged with Bubwith on the 18th for the archdeaooniy of Rich- 
mond. (Reg. Scrope, 8 5, 9 a.) This was a pleasant way of evading the difficulty 
of the papal provision. On the 18th of October, 1401, Scrope, then domestic chaplain 
to his uncle, was made by him the prebendary of Studley at Ripon. (Reg. Scrope, 4 a.) 
This he held till Jan. 1408-9, when he exchanged it with Thomas de Polton for the 
stall of Knaresbro' at York. (Reg. Bowet, 40 a.) Scrope was a residentiary at York, 
and is always styled '* junior '* to distinguish him from his father. 

On the 23rd of June, 1415, his ill-fiited brother Henry lord Scrope left him in his 
will *' nnum par tabellarum cerearum de argento, deauratum ; et unum librum de 
Omeliis S. Qeorgii ; et alium librum de Omeliis S. Remigii ; et alium libmm de Ome* 
His Yen. Bedie presbiteri ; et unum librum de Revelationibus S. BrigidsB Yii^ginis, 
quem emi Beverlaci, pro remembrancia." (Foed. ix. 277.)

XI. THE WILL OP JOHN PKOPHETE, DEAN OP YORK. 
[Reg. Test. Deo. et Cap. Ebor. i. 176.] 

London, April 8, 1416. Johannes Prophete,t decanus Ebor. 
— Corpus meum putridum tradendum ecclesiasticae sepulturae infra 

• A merchant and goldsmith of York. Free 1886. Bailiff 1887-8. Lord Mayor 
li07, 1408, and 1409. Died 5th August, 1419, and was buried at St. Crux. He 
married Agnes, daughter and co-heir of John de Barden, alderman of York. She 
died 22nd Sept. 1418. These dates are from a brass in the church of St. Cruz ; 
those in print are incorrect For an interesting accouiit of the Wymans see a notice 
pf the indulgence cup of archbishop Scrope, published in the Archa»ological Transac- 
tions, by R. Davies, F S.A.-— R.H.S. 

t John Prophete, dean of York, held a high position both in church and state. 

In 1889 and 1390 he occurs as clerk of the Privy Council. (Acts and Ord. of the 
Privy Council, i. 12, &c.) In the 6th of Henry IV. he occurs as the king's secretary 
(GaL Rot. Pat. 250), and, soon afterwards, he became keeper of the privy s^, in which 
capacity he was appointed one of the executors of the king^s will in 1 408. (Nicholses Royal 
Wills, 205; Cal. Rot. Pat. 259 ; Rot. Pari.) Many of his official letters as keeper 
of the privy seal are in MSS. Harl. No. 481. On the 12th of Nov. 1400, he was 
employed in some negociations connected with the restitution of queen Isabella (Fosd. 
viii. 164), and on the 18th of October, 1414, he was appointed ambassador to 
negociatea marriage with Katherine of France. (Ibid. ix. 182.) In that year he was 
one of the executors of Beatrix lady Rooe. (Test. Ebor. i. 878.) 

His ecclesiastical preferments were numerous. In 1882 he was rector of Adisham 
in Kent. (Hasted, iii. 671.) This he exchanged on the 11th of May, 1886, with Wil- 
liam Lye, for the rectory of Haseley (MSS. Harl. 6952, 10a) ; and he again exchanged 
Haseley, on Dec. 2nd, with Raymond Pelegrim, for the prebend of Milton at Lincoln. 
(Ibid. 106.) He resigned this stall in 1405, when be was appointed to that of Leighton 
Buzzard, in the same church. (Le Neve, ii. 171.) On the 7th of November, 1898, he 
was installed dean of Hereford, holding that office until 1407; in which year he gave 
up the prebends of Moreton, Piona Pan-a, and Warham and Ayleston in the same 
church. (Le Neve, i. 476, 515, 522, 529.) 

On the 22nd of October, 1404, archbishop Scrope collated him to the stall of 
Langtoft at York. (MSS. Torre.) This he exchanged with Thomas de Walleworth 
for the prebend of Bugthorpe, to which he was admitted by the Chapter, during the

XV. THB WILL OP ROGER WHELPDALE, BISHOP OP CARLISLE. 

[Reg. archiep. Bowet, pan i. 287 a &.] 

In Dei nomine, amen. Ego Rogerus, humilis minister, licet 
indignus, cathedralis ecclesiae Karliolensis,* vicesimo quinto die 
Januarii, in die, videlicet, Conversionis Sancti Pauli, Dei gratia 
solum confisus, corporaliter mentis compos, condo voluntatem 
meam testimonialem in hunc modum. Profiteer primo sancta; 

* Bishop Whelpdale, who makes the following pious and chaFscteristic disposition 
of his worldly effects, is said to have heen a native of Cumberland. He went to Ox- 
lord and became a fellow of Balliol College. (Hist. Oxford Colleges, 85.) Afterwards he 
was a fellow of Queen's (157), of which college he was made provost on the 15th of 
April, 1404 (146), the archbishop of York confirming his appointment on the 24th. 
(Reg. Sorope.) He resigned his office in 1420. He founded an eleemosynary chest 
in the college, to which he gave 86^. 16«. id. (Hist. Oxford Colleges. 157.) In 1403 
Whelpdale was one of the proctors for the University. (Appendix, 36.) 

In 1412 Whelpdale was presented by the bishop of Winchester to the living of 
Stockton in the diocese of Salisbury, which he resigned in the following year. 
(Phillippa' WUtshiie Incumbents, 102.) 

Whelpdale received the temporalities of the see of Carlisle on March 17th, 1419-20, 
and made his profession of obedience on August 1st. He died 4th Feb. 1422-3, and 
waa buried in St. Paul's cathedral. (Le Neve, iii. 238. Nicolson and I5urn, ii. 272.) 

Whelpdale is said to have written several treatises, particularly on mathematics and 
logic, which are mentioned in the usual text-books of literary biography.

CANON RESIDENTIARY OF YORK. 

[Reg. Test Dec. et Cap. Ebor. i. 262 b, and Orig. Inv.] 

Jan. 10, 1448. Thomas Morton,* clericus, et praebendarius 
prasbendae de North Newbalde, ac residentiarius in eccl. cath.

In 1433 he became prebendary of Stow Longa, at Lincoln, and gave it up when ap- 
pointed to th« sull of Sutton cum Bucks in July 1488. (Le Neve, ii. 217.) 

Dixon built the chancel of Cheshunt church, and, dying Oct. 30th, 1448, was buried 
there. A flne brass was placed over him, with a curiously rhyming epitaph. A por- 
tion of the canopy is engraved in Bouteirs Sepulchral Brasses. (See Newcourt, i. 820; 
Clutterbuck^s Herts, ii. 112; Gough^s Sepulchral Monuments, ii. 156, where tilie in- 
acription is correctly given.)

* On Augnst 28rd, 1423, Thomas Morton was admitted to the stall of North New- 
bald, at York, having exchanged for it with John Prentis his prebend of Alton Saint 
Pancras, at Salisbury, and that of Bolenhall, in the royal chapel at Tamworth. (Reg. 
Bowet, i. 79 fi.) He was installed in the person of John Ragenhill, Aug. 28tb, 1423, 
and, in his own person, on Sept. 10th, 1426. (Acta Capit. Ebor.) On the 9th of Jan. 
1429-30, he had permission from the chapter to be absent for thir^-one days at Lon- 
don, on their business, whilst he was in residence. (Ibid.) 

On April 14th, 1423, the archbishop of York ordered Morton to be inducted to the 
rectory of Almondbury, he having exchanged for it his prebend of Hinton, at Here> 
ford, with Thomas Woodford. (Reg. Bowet, i. 147a, b.) On July 8rd, 1427. he was 
ordered to be inducted to the rectory of Brompton, giving up for it bis rectory of 
Hafhunt (sic) and his stall at St. Stephen*s Westminster. (Reg. Kempe.) He owed many 
of his preferments, no doubt, to the fact of his being a retainer of the Cardinal of 
England. (Feed. x. 609.) From 1429, to the time of his death, he was master of 
Brackley Hospital, Northants. (Baker's Northants. i. 581.) On the 14th of April, 
1431, he exchanged his rectory of Brompton for that of Settrington, which he held 
during his life. (Reg. Kempe, 857 a.) On July 2lBt, 1434, he exchanged his stall of 
Sidlesham and Bishopston, at Chichester, with Walter Sherrington for the prebend of 
Barnby, at Howden. (Reg. Kenipc. 3776.) On the 2nd of March, 1435 6, he was 
instituted , at the presentation of Kirkham Priory, to the living of St. Peter in the 
Willows, at York, which he gave up in the following May. (Reg. Kempe, 480 6.) .

XXIX. THE WILL OF WILLIAM FELTER, DEAN OF YORK. 

(Beg. Test. Gapit. Ebor. i. 267 a.) 

April 6, 1451. Willelmus Felter,* decanus Eboracensis.^- 
sep. m ecd. cath. Ebor. Lego 1 li. ad usum ecclesise, reponendas 

* William Felter^ dean of York, aeemB to have been a natiTe of Bristol. I am un- 
acquainted with hiB early histoiy, but he was introduced to Yorkshire by archbishop 
Kempe, whose chancellor he was. On Feb. 20th, 1429-80, the primate gate him the 
stall at St. Peter's ahar at Beverley, which he resigned in Jan. 1450-1. (Reg. Kempe, 
8 b, 71 a.) On June 21st, 1485, he was collated to the archdeaconry of York (Ibid. 
15&.), in which he was installed in person on July 7th. (Acta cipit. Ebor.) In 
December, 1486, Felter became dean of York. On the last day of Feb., 1441-2, he 
was collated to the stall of Apesthorpe (Kempe, 47 a.), in which he was installed by 
proxy on 8th March, and in pereon on May 9th. (Acta Gapit. Ebor.) On Jan. 14th, 
1450-1, he was collated to the stall of Driffield (Reg. Kempe, 71 a.), and, on March 
15th, he was one of the persons appointed by the primate to act as bis vicar-genenl. 
He was rector of Almondbury at his death (Reg. Kempe, 74 bX and between 1407 
and 1485 he was dean of Wolverhampton. (MSS. Harl. 6952, 68 a. Shawns Stafford- 
shire, ii. 154.) 

On Feb. 5, 1485-6, Felter was one of the commissioners i^pointed to renew thip 
trace between England and Scotland. (Feed. z. 629; Rot. Scoti», ii. 294.) 

Felter died on the 10th of April, 1451, and was interred in the middle choir of 
York Minster, where an inscription in brass commemorated him. (Drake, 514.) He 
was a doctor of decrees. In 1454 his executors founded a chantry in the Minster at 
the altar of SS. Anne, Anthony, and Crux, for the dean*s soul, and those of John and

I find that William Duffield of York was ordained acolyte Feb. 19th, 1417-18; 
sobdeaoon March 12th, Trinity priory giving him a title ; deacon 21st May, 1418; 
and priest 11th March, 1418-19, — a very rapid progress. (Reg. Bowet) 

On May 5th, 1421, the king collated him to a stall in the cathedral of Lisienz 
(Feed. z. 112), and, on Oct. 27th, 1422, he was made rector of Gopford in Essex. 
(Newcourt, ii. 192.) On the 28rd of March, 1425, he was installed archdeacon of 
Colchester, and he held that oiftce until 1488. (Ibid. 189. Le Neve, ii. 340.) 

Duffield held several very lucrative and important offices in the diocese o^ Yoik, 
through the kindness of archbishop Kempe. On March 22nd, 1428>9, he was col- 
lated by him to a stall at Beverley. (R^. Kempe, 76.) On Sep. 17^ 1482, the same 
prelate appointed him prebendaiy of Norwell Overhall at Southwell. (Reg. Kempe, 
106.) This he resigned in Oct. 1450, but was re-appointed Nov. 7, 1451, and held 
that post till he died. On the 8rd of May, 1488, he wss colUted by the archbishop, 
whilst he was at Calais, to the stall of Wistow at York (Kempe, 116) and, in Sept. 
1484« to the archdeaconry of Cleveland. (Ibid. 15a.) 

Dnffield died, as appears from the title of his inventory, on the 7th of M«*ch, 
1452-3. There is, however, no monument to commemorate him in York minster. 
He was a penon of vast wealth, as may be seen from the inventory of his effects.

* The beautiful and striking will of a York dignitary, John Caatell. 
On Sept. 28rd, 1402, a person of the name of John Caatell was ordained subdeacon 
at York, the monastery of St. Andrew giving him a title (Reg. Scrope), and he, being 
a master of arts, was made deacon Sept. 18, 1406, receiving his title from the hospital 
of St. John, without the east gate at Oxford. (Reg. Dec. et Cap. sede vaeante, 802 b.) 
In 1405 John Castell of Univ. Coll. was a proctor at Oxford. (Le Neve, iii. 480.) 
About 1418 he became master of Univ. Coll. (Ibid. iii. f>87). and was made chancellor 
by patent dated AprU 17, 1422 (Ibid. iii. 467), and he held that office in 1425. (Hist. 
Univ. Oxon. v. 42.) In 1424 he was one of the executors of Ralph earl of Westmor- 
land. (Durham Wills, i. 73.) He was chaplain to Henry Y. (Hist. Univ. Oxon. v. 
42.; Smith's Annals of Univ. Coll. 164.) 

On Nov. 15th, 1428, he was made chancellor of Lincoln. (Le Neve, ii. 93.) On 
Sept. 15th, 1481, he was collated to the archdeaconry of Berkshire fibid. ii. 685), and 
held it for a year. On Sept. 2nd, 1480, he was appointed to the golden stall at Hereford 
(Ibid. i. 501), having become chancellor there on July 7, 1425. (Ibid. i. 492.) In 
1485 he resigned the stall of Carlton-cum-Kyme at Lincoln. (Ibid. ii. 121.) From 
1428 to 1480 he seems to have been rector of St Clement Danes, London. (New- 
court, i. 572.) 

In Yorkshire, on Oct 18, 1423, he was instituted to the rectory of Rudby on the 
death of Robert de Wydiffe, which he held until his death (Reg. Bo wet, i. 164 6); 
and, on Jan. 9, 1424-5, he was admitted to the stall of Skelton at Howden,- which he 
resigned in 1486. (Reg. sede vaeanle, 873 a.) On Feb. 12, 1435-6, he was admitted 
to the prebend of Wetwang and the rectoiy of Cottingham, exchanging for them with 
Nicholas Dixon his stall of Cheminste^ and Bere at Salisbury. (Reg. Kempe, 156.) 
On Oct 7, 1447, he was appointed precentor. On June 12th, 1447, the archbishop 
appointed a commission to receive his resignation of the living of Cottingham, which 
he gave up owing to old age and infirmities, and a pension out of it was granted to 
him. (Ibid, no a.) 

Castell died in one of the early months of 1457, and was buried in York minster, 
and the following striking epitaph commemorated him. (Drake, 499.) It was near 
the font in the nave on " a broad white stone, about three yards long, inscribed both 
on its veige and crossways.'* (MS. Torre, 148.) 

+ Hie jacet dom* Johannes Castell miser et indignus sacerdos.

belonged to the chantry chapel of St. Mary, mentioned in the testator's will. Sir Ran-

In the diocese of York Andrew held several pieces of preferment. On Nov. 29th, 
1445, archbishop Kempe collated him to the stall of Warthill at York. (Reg. Kempe, 
56 b.) This he gave up when he was collated to the prebend of North Newbald on 
August 19th, 1449. (Ibid. 66 6.) On July 28th, 1461, he exchanged his prebend 
of Fontenell at Shaftsbury with Andrew Holes, for one of the stalls of Oxton-cum- 
Crophill at Southwell. (Reg. Will. Booth, 53 a.) This he resigned on Nov. 10th, 
1476, receiving a retiring pension of 20 marks per ann. Thrice — on June 8th, 1465; 
March 2nd, 1474-5; and June 8th, 1475, he was made vicar-general. 

In 1451 William Fetter, dean of York, died, and Andrew was forced upon the 
chapter as his successor. That body selected their treasurer John Bemingham, and 
a long and painful struggle ensued, which resulted in the Minster being put under 
an interdict. Thomas (^Mcoigne boldly charges Andrew with carrying his point by 
bribeiy, but he was not formally installed as dean until the Ist of June, 1454. An 
aocM>nnt of the affair is to be found in the appendix to Heame's edition of Walter of 
Hemingburgh, ii. 522. Andrew held the office of dean for many years, and resigned 
it shortly before his death on July 8tb, 1477. 

In 1443 Andrew was made secretary to Henry VI. I say nothing here of the 
many services that he rendered to the state, or of the embassies on which he was 
sent.

* The founder of the liumily of Witham of Cliffe, and Lartington in Uie North 
Riding of Yorkshire. He is said to have been a son of Robert Witham of Grantham, 
but, as to the truth of this statement, some further evidence is required. He comes 
before us, however, as the nowt homo of a good old Yorkshire house, and it was 
through his influence and industry that its wealth and position were mainly secured. 
Witham was probably connected in esrly life with the fiimily of Neville, and he was 
executor of the earl of Salisbury and his son the king-maker. (Test. Ebor. ii. 240, 
246.) On March 16th, 1471*2, he was made a commissioner to treat with Scotland. 
TFced. zi. 748.) He was also concerned with the aflkirs of that countiy in 1478. 
(Ibid, 776, 786.) Witham's connection with the dominant family of the day made 
him employed more or less in public duties, and it will be found that he had tuik 
friends in the lords Salisbury and Warwick, and in Richard duke of Gloucester, after- 
wards Richard III. . From the windows of bis hall at Comburgh, he could look up 
to the stately towers of Sheriff button castle, which almost overdiadowed his humbler 
residence. He was thus in constant connexion with one of the principal residences 
of the noble house of Neville, which had befriended him for so many years, and which 
he had served so faithfully and so well. 

The chief distinction of Witham^s life was his holding the office of (Tbancellor of 
the Exchequer. He was thrice appointed to it by letters patent : 1st in 82nd Heniy 
YI ; again in 84th Henry YI; and, lastly, in th# 4th of Edward IY. On the second 
occasion he was appointed for life. (Gal. Rot Pat 296, 297, 807.) He would acquire 
this honour through the influence of the Nevilles.

Booth, 7 a &.) On March 5th, 1477-8, he was installed sub-dean of York. (Regg. 
Capit. et Laur. Booth, 5 a, etc.) This he held until his death, together with the rectory

The rector of Rudby was one of the younger children of Christopher Conyers, and 
was amply provided for in his will. He took orders somewhat late in life, and proba- 
bly with a view of being presented to the living of Rudby. On the 20th of Sept. 
1455, Chr. Conyers of Hornby was made acolyte; snbdeacon on 20 Dec., receiving 
his title from Easby abbey ; deacon on Febr 21 ; and priest on ISth March, seq<^ all 
within seven months. (Reg. Will. Booth.) On the last day but one of February* 
1456-7, he was instituted to the rectory of Rudby in Cleveland, on the presentation of 
Sir John Conyers, knt., his brother. This living he held till he died in the autumn of 
1483. (Reg. Will. Booth, 65 b.) In 1469 he was made a brother of the Corpus 
Christi guild at York. (MSS. Lansdowne, cccc.iii, 58 a.) On the 2Srd of November. 
1468, archbishop Neville allowed to Chr. Conyers the use of an oratory for a year. 
(Reg. i. 107 a.)

DISPENSATIONS FOR MARRUGE, MARRIAGE 

LICENCES, ETC. 



I now give a list of all the licences and dispensations for mar- 
riage, and the names of all the widows who took the vow of 
chastity, which appear in the registers of the archbishops of York, 
the biuiops of Durnam, and the archdeacons of Richmond. They 
are arranged in chronological order, beginning with the reign of 
Eichard II.; prior to which time there are few, if any, to be 
found. This series corers the whole tract of coimtry nrom the 
Humber to the Tweed, and the information which it affords is 
i\pyel and valuable, not only to the genealo^st, but also to the 
ecclesiastical antiquary. A Jtew words on each class of documents 
brought before my readers may be of some use. 

I. Marriage Licences. Marriages usually were celebrated after 
banns in the parish church of one of the two parties. Special 
leave, however, was necessary, if the two persons were to be 
married in a strange church ; or if the banns were to be asked 
twice, or only once. Sometimes they were asked thrice on the 
same day, for the sake of expedition. Leave, abo, was necessary, 
if the marriage was to take place in a private chapel or oratory. 
In that case, the incumbent of the parish was desired to allow it, 
and the bannd were previously askea in the parish church. 

II. Dispensations. If two persons desiring to marry were re- 
lated to.each other in the third or fourth degree of consanguinity; 
if one of the two had been sponsor to the otner, or a chila of the 
other, they could not marry without a dispensation, and this was 
to be obtained in the papal court. There were other connections 
also which rendered an alliance unlawfuL Supposing that they 
had married in ignorance of the tie between them, the marriage 
was illegal, and the issue of it illegitimate. This also could be 
remedied by an ex post facto dispensation. The dispensation was 
issued on this wise. The pope, or some member of the Sacred 
College acting in his behalf, listened to the case of the claimant, 
and, if it was proper, granted a dispensation legitimatising the 
marriage, past or future. This document, however, was not a 
final one. It was only to stand good in case that, after due exa- 
mination into the allegations contained in the petition by the 



312 TEST AMENTA EBORACBN8IA. 

bishop or archbishop at home, they were found to be correct, 
and in case that no improper influence had been brought to 
bear upon the woman to compel her to join in the petition. When 
the petitioner or his dispensation reached England, it was pre- 
sented to the prelate; and he, or his deputy, examined into the 
whole matter; and, if the statements of tne petitioner were found 
to be correct, the dispensation took effect at once, and was 
entered in the prelate's register, and issued with the addition of 
hh formal approval. In this examination the pedigrees of the 
two persons would be produced; and, on one or two occasions, 
they are entered on the register. It appears, also, that forged 
dispensations were sometimes offered ana made use of by the 
unwary recipients. In the case of the marriage of Sir Henry 
Scrope and Philippa Ros in 1398, I have printed the papal 
dispensation, and the other formal documents connected with it, 
as a specimen of the class. Occasionally, I believe, English 
bishops had authority from the pope to grant these dispensations 
without an immediate reference to the papal court. Thomas 
Langley, bishop of Durham, was allowed to do so in twelve 
cases. 

III. Vows of Chastity. A lady, after her husband's death, 
was allowed to take the vow of chastity, and she was then called 
a vowess. A kind of investiture took place, generally, I believe, 
during or before the celebration of mass, when the officiator 
gave the vowess a pall or mantle, a veil, and a ring, and she 
then made a vow of chastity in a set form of words. The cele- 
brant was not necessarily a Bishop, but an Abbat or a Prior 
might act in his stead. This* vow merely obliged the lady to 
live in chastity. She was not severed from the world, but could 
live in it and make a will, and dispose of her property as she 
chose. Wc sometimes find that the vowess, for the sake of a 
stricter and a more retired life, took up her abode in or near 
some monastery, particularly a nunnery. She was, however, 
merely a lodger, or, to use the old ienn^hperhendinaria. I have 
given many examples of the vows that were taken by these 
ladies. The whole subject opens out a new phase of mediaeval 
life.

THE SURTEES SOCIETY. 



REPORT FOR THE YEAR MD.COC.LXIV. 

IRead at the General Mt^ng on the Ith of June}. 

Thirty years have passed away since the Surtees Society was 
founded, and the members may well congratulate themselves 
on the position that it at present occupies. There are ups and 
downs in the history of every literary association ; there are 
times when workers become weary and supporters listless ; and 
then there is a crisis full of peril and discouragement, which 
is too oft^n fatal in its consequences. The Surtees Society is 
not unacquainted with these dangers, but it has had the good 
fortune to be uninjured by them. Not only has it the gratifi-: 
cation of being the oldest of the English Societies, but it has 
also the pride of feeling that, after thirty years spent in hard 
and honest work, it is still fiill of life and energy, eager to 
devise new plans and schemes, and anxious to cany them out. 

During the past year there have been twelve vacancies in 
the list of members, but this loss has been more than compen- 
sated for by the election of thirty-eight new associates. This 
is a most gratifying increase in our numbers, and yet it is not 
above the average of the last five or six years. Ten years ago 
we had only one hundred and fifty members, now we have as 
many as three hundred and thirty; and by a resolution passed 
at our last general meeting it was resolved that the number of 
associates should be limited to three hundred and fifty. By 
taking this step the Society hopes to attain and keep a fixed 
and steady basis on which it can work, without being either 
lead astray by ambition, or thwarted and dismayed by poverty. 

Not only have the additions to our list of members been so 
great, but the balance-sheet of the Treasurer is very decidedly 
in favour of the Society. The sale of the publications is large, 
and the more recent volumes have been speedily out of print 



This has induced the C!ouiicil to raise, in many instances, the 
prices of the volumes to non-subscribers. The Council 
lias no wish to afford facilities for purchasing them to the 
injury of the members ; and, in the present condition of the 
Society, every one must see that it will be very much to his 
interest to secure our publications as a subscriber and not as 
a stranger. , 

The Council is fully conscious that the chief reason for the 
great prosperity of the Society at the present time is the large 
and increasing support which it receives from the gentlemen 
of Yorkshire. From the fact that about half of the members 
of the Society are Yorkshiremen, the Council is rejoiced to 
see that not only are its Yorkshire works (published and pro- 
posed) properly appreciated, but, also, that its position as the 
literary association for that great county is fully recognised 
and understood. The Society will now be able to take in hand 
more Yorkshire subjects than it has liitherto been able to do; 
but it must still be remembered that there are other districts 
which have just claims upon its attention which cannot be 
passed over. 

There has, we are sorry to say, been a considerable delay in 
the issue of the publications of the Society for several years, 
but the nature of the subjects that have been taken in hand 
renders this delay unavoidable. No one can have any concep- 
tion of the toil and the research that are necessary to prepare 
anything in the shape of a chronicle for the press ; and every 
allowance ought to be made for an editor who is disposed to 
edit one with the care that it deserves. The labour and the 
expense of doing so are necessarily considerable; and nothing 
save a love for his subject and a true interest in the welfare 
and the reputation of the Society, can induce any one to take 
upon himself so great a burden. The kind forbearance that 
has been manifested by the members of the Society is a proof 
that they appreciate and are grateful for the labours of their 
editors. 

There are two works in progress for the current year. 

The first is a third volume of Wills from the Ilegistry at 
York, a series of very great interest. This volume will pro- 
bably end at the beginning of the reign of Henry VIII., and 
tliose who are conversant with the valuable documents which 
have been already drawn from that repository, will look for- 
ward with eager interest to a continuation of them. Some 
early Inventories, also, have been discovered, and will be pub- 
lished ; incliuling those of two Archbishoi>8 of York in the 



3 

fifteenth century. The vahie of the pictures of domestic life 
which these documents reveal to us cannot be over-estimated. 

The second is the concluding volume of the Memorials of 
the Priory of Hexham. This will contain an imprint of the 
Black Book of the Monastery, from the original in tlie pos- 
session of Mr. Beaumont, and all the deeds and grants con- 
nected with the possessions of the house and the local admi- 
nistration of the Regality that it has been possible to recover. 
There will also be in the volume an architectural description 
of the church illustrated with numerous engravings. Tlie 
chief renown of Hexham is in its Saxon history, and all the 
remains of that period that have been discovered in the place 
will be set forth in the volume. 

In addition to these two works, great progress has been 
made with others that will before long be presented to the 
members of the Society. A second volume of the Memorials 
of Fountains Abbey is now ready for the press ; and, through 
the kind munificence of Mr. Akroyd, it will be richly illus- 
trated with engravings. The Lives of St Wilfrid, and 
some other historical pieces, are, we are happy to say, 
being prepared by the Rev. William Stubbs. A third vol- 
ume of Durham and Northumberland Wills (to conclude 
the series) is being collected by the Rev. William Greenwell. 
The Council has also much pleasure in announcing for speedy 
publication the Letters and Household Books of Lord Wil- 
liam Howard of Naworth. Through the great kindness of 
the Earl of Carlisle these memorials of " Belted Will" have 
been placed at the disposal of the Society. We have been 
accustomed to look upon Lord William merely as a Border 
chieftain, but it is evident that he was a person of great re- 
finement and taste. Li spite of the misfortunes of himself 
and his family, he foimd time to gather together a collection 
of old Chronicles and MSS., and he took care that some of 
them were printed: he made a collection of pictures and 
works of art; he was an accomplished genealogist; and he 
corresponded with the famous Camden about Roman altars. 



THE SURTEES SOCIETY, 

ESTABUSUED IN THB TEAB 1884, 

III honour of die late Robert Surtees, of Mainsforth, EHquire, 
the Author of the History of the Countv Palatine of Durham, 
and in accordance with hid pursuits and plans ; having for its 
object the pubHcation of inedited Manuscripts, illustrative of 
the intellectual, the moral, the religious, and the social con- 
dition of those parts of England and Scotland, included on the 
east between the Humber and the Frith of Forth, and on the 
west between the Mersey and the Clyde, a region which con- 
stituted the ancient Kingdom of Northumbria. 

NEW RULES AQREED UPON IN 1849; REVISED 1863. 

I. The Society shall consist . of not more than three hun- 
dred and fifty members. 

XL There shall be a Patron of the Society, who shall be 
President 

III. Tliere shall be twenty-four Vice-Presidents, a Secre- 
tary, and two Treasurers. 

rV. The Patron, the Vice-Presidents, the Secretary, and 
the Treasurers, shall form the Council, any five of whom, 
including the Secretary and a Treasurer, shall be a quorum 
competent to transact the business of the Society. 

V. Tlie twenty-four Vice-Presidents, the Secretary, and 
the Treasurers, shall be elected at a general meeting, to con- 
tinue in office for three years, and be capable of re-election. 

VI. Any vacancies in the offices of Secretary or Treasurers 
shall be provisionally filled up by the Coimcil, subject to the 
approbation of the next general meeting. 

VIL Tliree meetings of the Council shall be held in every 
year, on the first Tuesday in the months of March, June, and 
December ; and the place and hour of meeting shall be fixed 
by the Council, and communicated by the Secretary- to the 
members of the Council. 

VIII. The meeting in June shall be the anniversary, to 
which all the members of the Society shall be convened by 
the Secretary. 

IX. The Secretary shall convene extraordinary meetings of 



the Council, on a requisition to that effect, signed by not less 
than five members of the Council, being presented to him. 

X. Members may be elected by ballot at any one of the 
ordinary meetings, according to priority of application^ upon 
being proposed in writing by three existing members. One 
black ball in ten shall exclude, 

XL Each member shall pay in advance to the Treasurer 
the annual sum of one guinea. If any member's subscription 
shall be in arrear for two years, and he shall neglect to pay 
his subscripton after having been reminded by the Treasurer, 
he shall be regarded as having ceased to be a member of the 
Society. 

XII. The money raised by the Society shall be expended 
in publishing such compositions, in their original language, or 
in a translated form, as come within the scope of this Society, 
without limitation of time with reference to the period of their 
respective authors. All editorial and otlier expenses to be de- 
frayed by the Society. 

'XIII. One volume, at least, in a closely printed octavo 
form, shall be supplied to each member of the Society every 
year, free of expense. 

XIV. If the funds of the Society in any year will permit, 
the Council shall be at liberty to print and furnish to the 
members, free of expense, any other volume or volumes of the 
same character, in the same or a different form. 

XV. The number of copies of each publication, and the 
selection of a printer and publisher, shall be left to the Council, 
who shall also fix the price at which the copies not furnished 
to members shall be sold to the public. 

XVI. The armorial bearings of Mr. Surtees and some other 
characteristic decoration connecting the Society with his 
name, shall be used in each pubUcation. 

XVII. A list of the officers and members, together witli an 
account of the receipts and expenses of the Society, shall be 
made up every year to the time of the annual meeting, and 
shall be submitted to the Society to be printed and published 
with the next succeeding volume, 

XVIII. No alteration shall be made in these rules except 
at an annual meeting. Notice of any such alteration shall be 
given, at least as early as the ordinary meeting of the Council 
immediately preceding, to be communicated to each member 
of the Societv.
